Giselle. A landmark Romantic ballet in two acts with music by Adolphe Adam and choreography originally created by Jean Coralli and Jules Perrot. The title character, Giselle, is a frail peasant girl with a weak heart who loves dancing despite her mother's warnings. She falls in love with a man calling himself Loys, who is actually Duke Albrecht disguising himself as a peasant to court her while hiding his royal identity and his betrothal to another woman named Bathilde. When the gamekeeper Hilarion reveals Albrecht's true identity, Giselle suffers a complete mental breakdown, the so-called mad scene, and dies of a broken heart. In the second act, Giselle joins the Wilis, a group of vengeful spirits composed of women who died before their wedding day. The Wilis force men to dance to their death in a forest, but Giselle's love for Albrecht proves so pure that she protects him from Myrtha, the Queen of the Wilis, by dancing with him until dawn breaks and the spirits' power fades. This ballet stands in stark contrast to the lighthearted Coppelia, which also features a peasant couple caught in romantic conflict, but Giselle's tragic tone established the aesthetic for Romantic ballet and influenced countless works that followed.
